section.heading: 2.8 Subspaces of ℝn
section.paragraph: This section focuses on important sets of vectors in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ called subspaces. Often subspaces arise in connection with some matrix $$A$$ , and they provide useful information about the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ . The concepts and terminology in this section will be used repeatedly throughout the rest of the book.1

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ is any set $$H$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ that has three properties:

list.item: For each $$\textbf{u}$$ and $$\textbf{v}$$ in $$H$$ , the sum $$\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}$$ is in $$H$$ .﻿
For each $$\textbf{u}$$ in $$H$$ and each scalar $$c$$ , the vector $$c\textbf{u}$$ is in $$H$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: In words, a subspace is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. As you will see in the next few examples, most sets of vectors discussed in Chapter 1 are subspaces. For instance, a plane through the origin is the standard way to visualize the subspace in Example 1. See Figure 1.

image.alt: A graph shows a tilted parallelogram plane resting on a three-dimensional axis.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: If $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ are in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ and $$H = \text{Span} \left\{ \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2} \right\}$$ , then $$H$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . To verify this statement, note that the zero vector is in $$H$$ (because $$0\textbf{v}_{1} + 0\textbf{v}_{2}$$ is a linear combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2})$$ . Now take two arbitrary vectors in $$H$$ , say,
$$\textbf{u} = s_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + s_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} \text{and} \textbf{v} = t_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + t_{2} \textbf{v}_{2}$$
Then
$$\textbf{u} + \textbf{v} = \left(\right. s_{1} + t_{1} \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{1} + \left(\right. s_{2} + t_{2} \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{2}$$

which shows that $$\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}$$ is a linear combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ and hence is in $$H$$ . Also, for any scalar $$c$$ , the vector $$c\textbf{u}$$ is in $$H$$ , because $$c\textbf{u} = c(s_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + s_{2}\textbf{v}_{2}) = (cs_{1})\textbf{v}_{1} + (cs_{2})\textbf{v}_{2}$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: If $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is not zero and if $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ is a multiple of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , then $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ simply span a line through the origin. So a line through the origin is another example of a subspace.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: A line $$L$$ not through the origin is not a subspace, because it does not contain the origin, as required. Also, Figure 2 shows that $$L$$ is not closed under addition or scalar multiplication.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: For $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n},$$ the set of all linear combinations of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . The verification of this statement is similar to the argument given in Example 1. We shall now refer to $$\text{Span} \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ as the subspace spanned (or generated) by $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Note that $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ is a subspace of itself because it has the three properties required for a subspace. Another special subspace is the set consisting of only the zero vector in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . This set, called the zero subspace, also satisfies the conditions for a subspace.
section.heading: Column Space and Null Space of a Matrix
section.paragraph: Subspaces of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ usually occur in applications and theory in one of two ways. In both cases, the subspace can be related to a matrix.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The column space of a matrix $$A$$ is the set $$\text{Col} A$$ of all linear combinations of the columns of $$A$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: If $$A = \begin{bmatrix} \textbf{a}_{1} & \cdots & \textbf{a}_{n} \end{bmatrix}$$ , with the columns in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ , then $$\text{Col} A$$ is the same as $$\text{Span} \{\textbf{a}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{a}_{n}\}$$ . Example 4 shows that the column space of an $$\mathbf{\mathit{m}} \times \mathbf{\mathit{n}}$$ matrix is a subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ . Note that $$\text{Col} A$$ equals $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ only when the columns of $$A$$ span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ . Otherwise, $$\text{Col} A$$ is only part of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 1 & {- 3} & {- 4} \\ {- 4} & 6 & {- 2} \\ {- 3} & 7 & 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\textbf{b} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 3 \\ {- 4} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Determine whether $$\textbf{b}$$ is in the column space of $$A$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The vector $$\textbf{b}$$ is a linear combination of the columns of $$A$$ if and only if $$\textbf{b}$$ can be written as $$A\textbf{x}$$ for some $$\textbf{x}$$ , that is, if and only if the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has a solution. Row reducing the augmented matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} A & \textbf{b} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ ,﻿

image.alt: A graph shows a tilted square labeled col A lying in the negative z axis with its top edge touching the origin.

example.paragraph: we conclude that $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ is consistent and $$\textbf{b}$$ is in $$\text{Col} \textit{ }A$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: The solution of Example 4 shows that when a system of linear equations is written in the form $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ , the column space of $$A$$ is the set of all $$\textbf{b}$$ for which the system has a solution.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The null space of a matrix $$A$$ is the set $$\text{Nul} A$$ of all solutions of the homogeneous equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: When $$A$$ has $$n$$ columns, the solutions of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ belong to $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , and the null space of $$A$$ is a subset of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . In fact, $$\text{Nul} A$$ has the properties of a subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .﻿

note.title: Theorem 12
note.heading: Theorem 12
note.paragraph: The null space of an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is a subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Equivalently, the set of all solutions of a system $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ of $$m$$ homogeneous linear equations in $$n$$ unknowns is a subspace of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .﻿

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: The zero vector is in $$\text{Nul} A$$ (because $$A\textbf{0} = \textbf{0}$$ ). To show that $$\text{Nul} A$$ satisfies the other two properties required for a subspace, take any $$\textbf{u}$$ and $$\textbf{v}$$ in $$\text{Nul} A$$ That is, suppose $$A\textbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$ and $$A\textbf{v} = \textbf{0}$$ . Then, by a property of matrix multiplication,
$$A \left(\right. \textbf{u} + \textbf{v} \left.\right) = A \textbf{u} + A \textbf{v} = \textbf{0} + \textbf{0} = \textbf{0}$$

Thus $$\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}$$ satisfies $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ , and so $$\textbf{u} + \textbf{v}$$ is in $$\text{Nul} A$$ . Also, for any scalar $$c , A \left(\right. c \textbf{u} \left.\right) =$$ $$c\left( A\textbf{u} \right) = c\left( \textbf{0} \right) = \textbf{0}$$ , which shows that $$c\textbf{u}$$ is in $$\text{Nul} A$$ .﻿

To test whether a given vector $$\textbf{v}$$ is in $$\text{Nul} A$$ , just compute $$A\textbf{v}$$ to see whether $$A\textbf{v}$$ is the zero vector. Because $$\text{Nul} A$$ is described by a condition that must be checked for each vector, we say that the null space is defined implicitly. In contrast, the column space is defined explicitly, because vectors in $$\text{Col} A$$ can be constructed (by linear combinations) from the columns of $$A$$ . To create an explicit description of $$\text{Nul} A$$ , solve the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ and write the solution in parametric vector form. (See Example 6.)2
section.heading: Basis for a Subspace
section.paragraph: Because a subspace typically contains an infinite number of vectors, some problems involving a subspace are handled best by working with a small finite set of vectors that span the subspace. The smaller the set, the better. It can be shown that the smallest possible spanning set must be linearly independent.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A basic for a subspace $$H$$ of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ is a linearly independent set in $$H$$ that spans $$H$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: The columns of an invertible $$n \times n$$ matrix form a basis for all of $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ because they are linearly independent and span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , by the Invertible Matrix Theorem. One such matrix is the $$n \times n$$ identity matrix. Its columns are denoted by $$\textbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{e}_{n}$$ :

$$\textbf{e}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{e}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \ldots , \textbf{e}_{n} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
The set $$\{\textbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{e}_{n}\}$$ is called the standard basis for $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . See Figure 3.

image.alt: A figure shows three vectors along the three-dimensional axis.

figure.caption: Figure 3 The standard basis for ℝ3

section.paragraph: The next example shows that the standard procedure for writing the solution set of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ in parametric vector form actually identifies a basis for $$\text{Nul} A$$ This fact will be used throughout Chapter 5.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find a basis for the null space of the matrix
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, write the solution of $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ in parametric vector form:

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \\ x_{4} \\ x_{5}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 x_{2} + x_{4} - 3 x_{5} \\ x_{2} \\ - 2 x_{4} + 2 x_{5} \\ x_{4} \\ x_{5}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = x_{2} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. + x_{4} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ 0 \\ - 2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{matrix} \left]\right. + x_{5} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}- 3 \\ 0 \\ 2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. & & \begin{matrix} & & \end{matrix} \begin{matrix} & & & & & \end{matrix} \begin{matrix} & & \begin{matrix}\begin{matrix}\begin{matrix} & \end{matrix}\end{matrix}\end{matrix} & \begin{matrix}\end{matrix} \begin{matrix}\uparrow \\ u\end{matrix} & & \end{matrix} \begin{matrix} & \begin{matrix}\end{matrix} \begin{matrix}\uparrow \\ v\end{matrix} & & & & \end{matrix} \begin{matrix}\end{matrix} \begin{matrix} \begin{matrix}\uparrow \\ w\end{matrix}\end{matrix} & = & x_{2} \mathbf{u} + x_{4} \mathbf{v} + x_{5} \mathbf{w}$$

Equation (1) shows that $$\text{Nul} A$$ coincides with the set of all linear combinations of $$\textbf{u} ,$$ $$\textbf{v},$$ and $$\textbf{w}.$$ That is, $$\{\textbf{u},\textbf{v},\textbf{w}\}$$ generates $$\text{Nul} A$$ . In fact, this construction of $$\textbf{u} ,$$ $$\textbf{v},$$ and $$\textbf{w}$$ automatically makes them linearly independent, because equation (1) shows that $$\textbf{0} = x_{2}\textbf{u} + x_{4}\textbf{v} + x_{5}\textbf{w}$$ only if the weights $$x_{2} ,$$ $$x_{4},$$ and $$x_{5}$$ are all zero. (Examine entries $$2$$ , $$4$$ , and $$5$$ in the vector $$x_{2}\textbf{u} + x_{4}\textbf{v} + x_{5}\textbf{w}$$ .) So $$\{\textbf{u},\textbf{v},\textbf{w}\}$$ is a basis for $$\text{Nul} A$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Finding a basis for the column space of a matrix is actually less work than finding a basis for the null space. However, the method requires some explanation. Let’s begin with a simple case.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Find a basis for the column space of the matrix
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Denote the columns of $$B$$ by $$\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{5}$$ and note that $$\textbf{b}_{3} = - 3\textbf{b}_{1} + 2\textbf{b}_{2}$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{4} = 5\textbf{b}_{1} - \textbf{b}_{2}$$ . The fact that $$\textbf{b}_{3}$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{4}$$ are combinations of the pivot columns means that any combination of $$\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{5}$$ is actually just a combination of $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{b}_{5}$$ . Indeed, if $$\textbf{v}$$ is any vector in $$\text{Col} B$$ , say,
$$\textbf{v} = c_{1} \textbf{b}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{b}_{2} + c_{3} \textbf{b}_{3} + c_{4} \textbf{b}_{4} + c_{5} \textbf{b}_{5}$$
then, substituting for $$\textbf{b}_{3}$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{4}$$ , we can write $$\textbf{v}$$ in the form

$$\textbf{v} = c_{1} \textbf{b}_{1} + c_{2} \textbf{b}_{2} + c_{3} \left(\right. - 3 \textbf{b}_{1} + 2 \textbf{b}_{2} \left.\right) + c_{4} \left(\right. 5 \textbf{b}_{1} - \textbf{b}_{2} \left.\right) + c_{5} \textbf{b}_{5}$$

which is a linear combination of $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{b}_{5}$$ So $$\left\{ \textbf{b}_{1} \right.$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , $$\left. \textbf{b}_{5} \right\}$$ spans $$\text{Col} B$$ Also, $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{b}_{5}$$ are linearly independent, because they are columns from an identity matrix. So the pivot columns of $$B$$ form a basis for $$\text{Col} B$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: The matrix $$B$$ in Example 7 is in reduced echelon form. To handle a general matrix $$A,$$ recall that linear dependence relations among the columns of $$A$$ can be expressed in the form $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ for some $$\textbf{x}$$ . (If some columns are not involved in a particular dependence relation, then the corresponding entries in $$\textbf{x}$$ are zero.) When $$A$$ is row reduced to echelon form $$B$$ , the columns are drastically changed, but the equations $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ and $$B\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ have the same set of solutions. That is, the columns of $$A$$ have exactly the same linear dependence relationships as the columns of $$B$$ .﻿

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: It can be verified that the matrix

$$A = \begin{bmatrix} \textbf{a}_{1} & \textbf{a}_{2} & \hdots & \textbf{a}_{5} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 & 3 & 2 & - 9 \\ - 2 & - 2 & 2 & - 8 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 & 0 & 7 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & - 1 & 11 & - 8 \end{bmatrix}$$
is row equivalent to the matrix $$B$$ in Example 7. Find a basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: From Example 7, the pivot columns of $$A$$ are columns $$1$$ , $$2$$ , and $$5$$ . Also, $$\textbf{b}_{3} = - 3\textbf{b}_{1} + 2\textbf{b}_{2}$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{4} = 5\textbf{b}_{1} - \textbf{b}_{2}$$ . Since row operations do not affect linear dependence relations among the columns of the matrix, we should have
$$\textbf{a}_{3} = - 3 \textbf{a}_{1} + 2 \textbf{a}_{2} \text{and} \textbf{a}_{4} = 5 \textbf{a}_{1} - \textbf{a}_{2}$$

Check that this is true! By the argument in Example 7, $$\textbf{a}_{3}$$ and $$\textbf{a}_{4}$$ are not needed to generate the column space of $$A$$ . Also, $$\left\{ \textbf{a}_{1},\textbf{a}_{2},\textbf{a}_{5} \right\}$$ must be linearly independent, because any dependence relation among $$\textbf{a}_{1} ,$$ $$\textbf{a}_{2},$$ and $$\textbf{a}_{5}$$ would imply the same dependence relation among $$\textbf{b}_{1} ,$$ $$\textbf{b}_{2},$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{5}$$ . Since $$\left\{ \textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2},\textbf{b}_{5} \right\}$$ is linearly independent, $$\left\{ \textbf{a}_{1},\textbf{a}_{2},\textbf{a}_{5} \right\}$$ is also linearly independent and hence is a basis for $$\text{Col} A$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: The argument in Example 8 can be adapted to prove the following theorem.

note.title: Theorem 13
note.heading: Theorem 13
note.paragraph: The pivot columns of a matrix $$A$$ form a basis for the column space of $$A$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: Warning: Be careful to use pivot columns of $$A$$ itself for the basis of $$\text{Col} A$$ . The columns of an echelon form $$B$$ are often not in the column space of $$A$$ . (For instance, in Examples 7 and 8, the columns of $$B$$ all have zeros in their last entries and cannot generate the columns of $$A$$ .)
